blocks.text: What an AI assistant for technical writers should do on a Mac

A useful assistant for technical writers does four jobs well. It answers questions about the screen in front of you. It shows you where things are. It drafts or types text when you ask. It runs research while you keep writing. Most AI tools do one of these in a chat window. Few do all four inside the apps you already use.

The chat window is where most of the friction sits. You copy text out of Word or Google Docs. You paste it into a chat. You copy the answer back and fix the formatting. That loop costs time, and it pulls you away from the page. An assistant that sees your screen skips most of those steps.

Lazur takes that approach. Hold ⌥ ⌘ to ask about anything on screen, and Lazur answers out loud. It looks at the screen and listens only while you hold the shortcut. You keep your place in the document. You also keep the final say over every word that ships.
Where a technical writer's day actually goes

The U.S. Bureau of Labor Statistics lists the core duties of technical writers. You identify user needs. You work with product and technical staff. You write or revise support content and edit other writers' material. You add graphics, choose formats such as a manual or a video, and collect user feedback. Most of those duties depend on other people answering you.

Writing is only part of the week. Microsoft's 2023 Work Trend Index found that the average employee spends 57% of their time communicating in meetings, email and chat. The same study found that 43% goes to creating documents, spreadsheets and presentations. Those numbers describe the general office workforce. They are not a measure of technical writing.

The split comes from Microsoft 365 activity over a 28-day period, excluding weekends. The survey covered 31,000 full-time workers across 31 markets. Read it as a signal about office time, not as a rule for your team.
Why no current survey tells you how much time goes to docs

We looked for a recent number and did not find one. The Write the Docs 2025 salary survey drew 755 responses. It dropped its question about how much work time went to documentation. The answers could not be reliably related to salary, so the question went. No current study shows what a typical documentation week looks like.

You have to measure your own week. Keep a simple log for one working week. Mark each block of time as writing, reviewing, meeting, email or waiting. Waiting is the category most writers undercount. A page sits in review. A question sits in an engineer's inbox. Those hours vanish without a trace.

At the end of the week, add up the waiting time. Count the questions you asked and the people who answered them. Count the days a draft sat before anyone read it. That log tells you more than any industry average. It also shows where an assistant can help and where it cannot.
Voice help for the screen you are looking at

Hold ⌥ ⌘ and ask about the window in front of you. Lazur answers out loud. Ask a plain question, such as 'What does this error mean?' or 'Which option changes the page size?' Lazur reads what is on screen and answers. You do not need to copy anything first.

Two kinds of question come up most. The first asks where something is. Lazur draws a circle and a label around the item, so you see it without hunting. The second asks how to do something. Lazur guides you one click at a time and waits for each click before it moves on.

Guide mode helps most when you are new to an app or to a menu you open twice a year. Describe the goal in plain words. You do not need the exact menu name. Lazur explains each step and waits while you do it.

Here is a common case. You are in Word, and a reviewer wants tracked changes turned on. Ask: 'Where do I turn on tracking for this reviewer?' Lazur points at the Review tab and explains the next choice. You make each click yourself. The page stays exactly as you left it until you decide.
Dictate text at the cursor with fn in any app

Hold fn to dictate. Lazur types clean, formatted text at the cursor in any app. That can be a Notion page, a Google Doc, a Word file or a comment in a code editor. You stay in the window you are working in. You do not switch apps to paste.

Dictation works best for first drafts of prose. Speak the sentence the way you would explain it to an engineer. Then fix the few words that need changing. Editing a spoken draft is often quicker than typing from a blank page. Plan a short review pass after each session.

Set up a personal dictionary before your first big session. Add product names, API names, flag names and acronyms. Dictation guesses on unfamiliar words. Dictionary entries fix the spelling the next time you say them.

Snippets handle boilerplate. Store the standard prerequisites line, the warning block wording and your notice header. Clipboard slots keep a few pieces of text ready at once. Keep each snippet short, so you can check it at a glance before it goes into a page.
Draft from rough notes without losing control of the facts

Drafting is where the risk sits. A draft can read well and still be wrong. An assistant does not know how your product behaves unless you tell it. Give it the source. Paste in the change ticket, the release note or the engineer's message. Then ask for the draft.

Ask for a draft with limits. For example: 'Draft a two-sentence deprecation notice for the v2 endpoint. Use only the dates in my notes. Do not add a migration step.' Short, bounded prompts leave you less to fix. Long, open prompts give the model room to invent detail.

Check the dates, the version numbers and the commands first. Those are the parts readers act on. Compare each date with the ticket. Run each command or read it against the code. Check the tone last, against your style guide.
Note which sentences came from the source and which you wrote. The reviewer can then focus on the new text. A short comment at the top of the page saves a round of questions.
Research in the background while you keep writing

Some questions take longer than a glance. How do other vendors document rate limits? What do competitors call the same setting? Ask Lazur to research it. The research runs in Lazur's own Chrome tabs. Your document stays where you left it.

When the research finishes, you get a summary and a report. Read the report before you use any claim from it. Check the source link, the date on the page and whether the page covers your product version. Vendor pages change without notice.

Research helps most with comparison notes and style checks. It helps less with facts about your own product. Your engineers should confirm those. Treat a research report as a reading list with a summary attached.
Where Word, Google Docs, Notion and Markdown fit

Word is a common choice for long manuals. Lazur points at the Styles gallery, the Review tab and the other controls you use most. Heading structure matters for a table of contents and for navigation. Read [how to apply heading styles in Word](/how-to/apply-heading-styles-in-word) and the [Word guide for technical writers](/for/technical-writers/word).

Google Docs is common for shared drafts. Comments and suggestions are the main review tools. Read [how to add a comment in Google Docs](/how-to/add-a-comment-in-google-docs) and [how to accept or reject suggestions in Google Docs](/how-to/accept-or-reject-suggestions-in-google-docs). The [Google Docs guide for technical writers](/for/technical-writers/google-docs) covers shortcuts and templates.
Notion works well for team wikis and short internal pages. Callouts mark warnings and tips well. See [how to add a callout in Notion](/how-to/add-a-callout-in-notion).

Many docs-as-code teams write in Markdown. VS Code supports Markdown files out of the box with a built-in preview. On a Mac, press ⇧⌘V (Shift+Command+V) to switch the view. Lazur can point at the preview controls, explain the output and dictate prose into the editor.

blocks.title: Check your app version
blocks.text: Menu names and button labels change between app versions. Ask Lazur to point at the control you see on screen, not the name in this guide.
Lazur works the same way in each of these apps. It does not plug into any of them. It sees the screen and speaks. You do the typing, the formatting and the clicks, unless you dictate.
A worked example: from release note to published page
Here is one afternoon, start to finish. A release lands on Thursday. The change adds a required field to the create call. You need a page and a migration note ready for review on Friday.

items: Hold ⌥ ⌘ and ask what changed in the release note on screen. Lazur answers out loud.
Hold fn and dictate a summary of the change into a new page. Lazur types it at the cursor.
Ask Lazur to draft the migration note from your dictated summary. Keep the request short.
Check the new field name, type and default against the engineer's ticket. Fix anything that does not match.
Ask Lazur where the heading style control is, then apply the heading yourself.
Ask Lazur to research how other vendors describe the same change. Read the report and open its sources.
Ask Lazur to remind you of the review meeting. Lazur adds it to Apple Reminders.
Save the page, then send it for review with a note that lists what changed.

blocks.text: The useful part is the checks, not the speed. Lazur helped you find things and write the first pass faster. You still owned the field name, the default value and the date. Those are the lines a reader will act on.
What to do when the answer is wrong or the screen is unclear

Sometimes the answer is wrong. The menu may have moved in a newer version of the app. A dialog may hide the item you need. Say what you see. Ask again with the exact label on screen, such as the button text you can read.

If Lazur points at the wrong place, do not argue with it. Ask it to describe the window again. Then hold ⌥ ⌘ and ask for the label of the toolbar above the item. Short follow-up questions usually fix a mix-up.

Watch for the edge cases that matter in documentation. Two windows can show two versions of the same page. Name the window and the version you mean before you ask. Otherwise the answer may describe the wrong one.
Use the answer as a lead, not a verdict. Open the menu yourself and confirm the item exists. Then write the step into your page. That habit takes seconds and prevents a bad step in print.
Mistakes writers make with an AI assistant
Most problems come from habits, not from the tool. These are the ones to watch for.

items: Trusting a fluent draft without checking the version numbers and commands.
Pasting unreleased roadmap text into a tool your employer has not approved.
Asking a broad question and accepting the first answer you get.
Dictating code samples and pasting them without reading them back.
Quoting a research report without opening the source it cites.
Skipping peer review because the assistant sounds sure of itself.

blocks.text: Each mistake has the same fix. Slow down at the facts, and speed up at the wording. An assistant is good at the wording. You are responsible for the facts.
Privacy, confidential content and your employer's rules

Lazur listens and looks at the screen only while you hold the shortcut. Audio and the screenshot go to AI providers to answer your question. They are not stored. Content is never used to train AI models. Those are the product's rules.

Technical writers often see unreleased features, security details and customer data. Your employer's rules come first. Ask your security or legal team which AI tools you may use, and on which screens. Keep sensitive screens out of the assistant unless your employer allows it.

This page does not claim a compliance certification for any industry. If you write regulated documents, such as medical device instructions or financial disclosures, check your team's policy before you rely on any AI tool. Your team decides what counts as allowed.
What Lazur does not do

Lazur does not click buttons for you. It does not edit your files or operate other apps. It is not a plugin or add-in for Word, Google Docs, Notion or any other app. It has no partnership with any app maker. It guides, points, explains, answers out loud, drafts and types text.
That limit suits documentation work. You keep the edits, the formatting choices and the final check. Lazur saves time on the search, the recall and the first draft. You decide what goes live.
Try it on one documentation task this week
Start with one page that needs a change. Use ⌥ ⌘ to ask about it on screen. Hold fn to dictate the first paragraph of the update. Ask for a guide when you reach a menu you rarely open.

[Download Lazur](/download) for your Mac. The free trial starts when you first open the app, and it needs no credit card. Check the [pricing page](/pricing) before you choose a plan. Then judge it on your own week, not on a demo.

faq.question: What is the best AI assistant for technical writers on Mac?
faq.answer: There is no single best tool for every writer. Lazur is a voice assistant that works across the Mac apps you already use. It points, guides, explains, dictates and drafts. Compare it against your own week, including the apps you open most, before you pay.

faq.question: Does Lazur edit my Word or Google Docs files?
faq.answer: No. Lazur does not edit your files, click buttons or operate other apps. It points at things, guides you one click at a time, dictates text at your cursor when you hold fn, and drafts text you can review and paste.

faq.question: Can an AI assistant write documentation without errors?
faq.answer: Not on its own. Give it the source, such as the ticket or the code. Then check every date, version number, name and command. Treat the draft as a fast first pass that still needs a reviewer.

faq.question: Does Lazur watch my whole screen all the time?
faq.answer: No. Lazur looks at the screen and listens only while you hold the shortcut. Audio and the screenshot go to AI providers to answer, and they are not stored. Content is never used to train AI models.

faq.question: Is Lazur available on Windows?
faq.answer: Not yet. Lazur runs on macOS, on Apple silicon and Intel Macs. Windows is planned, but it is not available.

faq.question: Can I use Lazur with Markdown in VS Code?
faq.answer: Yes, for the parts you can see on screen. Lazur can point at the controls, explain what is on screen and dictate prose into the editor. VS Code's own Markdown preview is separate. On a Mac, press ⇧⌘V to switch the view.

faq.question: Do I need to check with my employer before I use an AI assistant?
faq.answer: Yes. Many teams have rules for AI tools and for confidential content. Ask before you use any tool on unreleased product screens, customer data or security details.

faq.question: Why does dictation miss product names?
faq.answer: Dictation guesses on words it has not seen before. Add product names, API names, flag names and acronyms to your personal dictionary. The spelling then stays correct the next time you say the word.

faq.question: How do I get started on my Mac?
faq.answer: Download the app and open it once. The free trial starts then, with no credit card. Press ⌥ ⌘ on a page you already have open, ask one question, then hold fn to dictate one paragraph.
